newsitem.title: USA: Coffee, grain prices drop on good weather.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, grain prices drop on good weather.

text.p: Coffee prices fell to the lowest level in a month on Tuesday as weather forecasts calling for milder temperatures in Brazil sparked a rush to exit the market by speculators that turned into a stampede.
In other markets, most grain prices also fell as Midwest growing weather improved and copper prices rallied after signs of rising industrial consumption from warehouse stocks.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery plummeted 35.35 cents a pound -- nearly 14 percent -- to end at 217.95 cents, the lowest closing price since May 9.

The July contract had shot up 16 cents on Monday on fears that a freeze might hit coffee trees in Brazil, the world's top producer. Prices had been retreating from a 20-year high of 318 cents on May 29 as Brazil's winter weather stayed mild.
"Yesterday's rally was on rumors of frost," said Allendale analyst Jim Cordier. "The non-frost event allowed coffee to trade where it wants to -- lower."
Officials at Brazilian coffee cooperatives said on Tuesday morning there were no reports of frost on coffee farms.
Weather forecasters now expect temperatures in the country's key coffee regions to rise slowly in coming days, with no forecasts of damaging cold in the near term.
Analysts said selling was also encouraged by a lack of buying in futures by coffee roasters, who are now thought to be fairly well supplied for the near term.

"I think it's lacking buyers," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "There has been a loosening of supply availability as Brazil's harvest proceeds and some of the mid-crop (or Mitaca) comes out of Colombia."
At the Chicago Board of Trade, improving crop weather in the Midwest also served to keep pressure on grain prices.
Soybeans for November delivery closed 12 cents a bushel lower at $6.67 and December delivery corn fell 2-1/2 cents to $2.55-1/2, reflecting the better prospects for big crops at the autumn harvest.

Rumors of buying interest from China, however, kept nearby prices for soybeans firm. July delivery soybeans ended 2 cents a bushel higher at $8.13 and July soybean meal closed up $1.90 a ton at $266.70.
There were reports on Tuesday that China bought up to 200,000 metric tons each of soybeans and soymeal this week.

"The fact is that there is still demand around for old crop supplies," said Jerry Gidel, grain analyst with Dean Witter brokerage in Chicago. "The Chinese are buying some meal out there for July, August and September shipment."

Wheat for July delivery closed down 4-1/2 cents a bushel at $3.63 as a crop tour of eastern Midwest wheat fields reported disease-free, healthy stands of winter wheat. The crop will be harvested next month.

Copper prices closed higher on the heels of a rally at the London Metal Exchange after stockpiles of copper in LME warehouses fell by 2,750 metric tons on Tuesday after a 1,750 ton drop the day before, signs of strong industrial demand.
Copper for July delivery at the COMEX in New York rose 2.55 cents a pound to close at 120.10 cents, its highest price in a year.
While copper stocks remain relatively tight worldwide, a seasonal downturn in demand over the summer could limit the market's upside potential, said Smith Barney analyst David Rineheimer.

Traders continued to monitor an ongoing strike at the Inco mining complex in Sudbury, Ontario. Workers there, who produce about 90,000 tons of copper annually, have been on strike since the beginning of the month.
Oil prices closed little changed ahead of the latest weekly production and stocks data from the American Petroleum Insitute, due after the close of trading on Tuesday.
Crude oil for July delivery ended down one cent at $18.67 a barrel, with July unleaded gasoline closing up 0.20 cent a gallon at 56.40 cents and July heating oil up 0.15 cent a gallon at 51.65 cents.
The API report was expected to show that refinery runs remained at or near record levels seen last week.

"Refineries are still chugging along at a great rate and it wouldn't take more than a pause in the import schedule to trim some of the inventory excess," said Tim Evans, an analyst at Pegasus Econometrics.
